strengths: The paper is well motivated: the observation that moiré artifacts manifest differently in high-frequency (texture) and low-frequency (color) components is clearly supported by the 2D/3D RGB curve visualizations in Fig. 2, and the dual-branch design directly follows from this analysis.

Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art on FHDMi across PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS and competitive on UHDM (first in SSIM and LPIPS, near-best in PSNR) with a compact 6.065M parameter model and low FLOPs (2.49 TFLOPS for 4K), demonstrating a good efficiency-performance trade-off.

Extensive and reasonably well-designed ablations covering the resize-vs-crop training strategy (Tab. 3, cross-validated with ESDNet-L), the learnable FCT, per-branch performance (Tab. 5), hierarchical fusion and RDDB (Tab. 6), and frequency decomposition choice.
The comparison with retrained general-purpose restoration models (OSEDiff, AdaIR, MoCE-IR) strengthens the case that the task-specific design matters, and includes parameter counts for fairness.
The crop/resize asymmetric training strategy is a simple, practical, and empirically validated idea for high-resolution demoiréing.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The frequency decomposition (Eq. 1-2) is a Gaussian blur/laplacian-style pyramid explicitly inspired by [37], the SA-CA module is essentially Restormer-style channel attention plus an RDDB (both adopted from prior work), and the FCT is a small fusion transformer. The overall contribution is more a well-engineered combination of known components than a new technique.

The Haar-transform ablation (PSNR 13.32, SSIM 0.2113) is implausibly bad and reads as a training/configuration failure rather than an inherent limitation of wavelet decomposition; the comparison with [10] may be unfair and undermines the claimed superiority of the proposed decomposition.
P-BiC [9], a recent UHDM-relevant method discussed in the related work and explicitly motivating the SA-CA design, is absent from the quantitative comparisons, weakening the SOTA claim on UHDM.

Some component ablations show marginal gains: hierarchical fusion and RDDB improve PSNR by only ~0.03 dB (Tab. 6), and the fixed-vs-learnable FCT difference is small (Tab. 4), raising questions about how much of the improvement comes from these advertised modules versus the resize-training strategy and overall capacity.

The two-stage training pipeline (separate branch training, then joint fine-tuning with feature-space crop alignment of the low-branch output) adds engineering complexity, and the robustness of this pipeline to hyperparameter choices is not analyzed.

Writing quality needs attention: several typos and informal phrasing ('awesome benifits', 'reals', 'effected'), and the sentence asserting equivalence of split convolutions to concatenation 'but doubles the number of bias parameters' is confusingly stated.

The paper is positioned as an efficient/edge-deployable model, but deployment-oriented evidence is thin: no latency measurements on edge hardware, and inference on the low branch still requires upsampling the 512-resolution feature back to full resolution, whose impact on extreme cases is not fully characterized.

strengths: Empirically strong results: Freqformer achieves the best reported numbers on FHDMi across PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS and is best or second-best on UHDM, while using only ~6M parameters and ~2.5 TFLOPs on 4K inputs, which is a genuinely good efficiency trade-off.

Reasonably comprehensive ablations: the paper studies the resize-vs-crop training strategy for the low-frequency branch (Tab. 3), the learnable FCT and two-stage training (Tab. 4), per-branch performance against a matched-size ESDNet (Tab. 5), and the hierarchical fusion/RDDB components (Tab. 6).

The core motivation is sensible and supported by qualitative evidence (Fig. 2): separating moiré into high-frequency texture and low-frequency color distortion is a plausible decomposition for this task, and the crop/resize training strategies follow naturally from the claimed properties.
Comparison with recent general-purpose restoration models (OSEDiff, AdaIR, MoCE-IR) both zero-shot and retrained is a useful and somewhat unusual addition for this subfield.
The code is stated to be publicly available, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The decomposition (Eqs. 1-2) is essentially a multi-level difference-of-Gaussians (separable binomial blur) pyramid, borrowed from [37] and well-known in classical vision; the dual-branch design, deep supervision, and residual connection follow FHDe2Net/MBCNN; resize-based scale-robust training largely follows ESDNet; and the SA-CA block is a Restormer-style channel attention with a gated FFN plus an off-the-shelf RDDB. The paper is a competent combination of existing components rather than a new idea.

The headline ablation against Haar wavelets is not convincing. A drop to 13.32 PSNR / 0.21 SSIM when swapping the decomposition for a 2-level Haar transform is so catastrophic that it almost certainly reflects an unfair or broken baseline implementation (e.g., incorrect inverse transform or training setup), rather than demonstrating the superiority of the proposed decomposition. This weakens the central claim against wavelet methods.

Key quantitative evidence is thin in places: the learnable FCT improves PSNR by only ~0.13 dB over fixed composition (Tab. 4), and hierarchical fusion improves by only ~0.03 dB (Tab. 6) — these are within typical run-to-run variance and no error bars or repeated runs are reported.

Incomplete comparison with the most relevant recent demoiréing methods: P-BiC [9] and the real-time mobile method [16] are discussed in the related work and used to motivate the design (SA-CA is explicitly inspired by [9]) but are absent from the quantitative tables, undermining the state-of-the-art claim. On UHDM the method is actually second in PSNR behind ESDNet-L.

The efficiency claims are not fully substantiated: 'suitable for deployment on edge devices' is asserted repeatedly but no edge-device latency, memory, or real deployment measurements are provided; only GPU FLOPs are reported. The two-branch pipeline with a resize and a crop path plus a joint fine-tuning stage also complicates training relative to single-stage baselines, which is not accounted for in the efficiency narrative.

Presentation quality is below the bar for ECCV: notable typos and informal language ('awesome benifits', 'reals that the green channel is less effected', a broken code URL in the abstract), a partially illegible pipeline figure (Fig. 3), an odd and confusing claim that adding two convolution outputs 'doubles the number of bias parameters' (they are equivalent, so the double-bias version is strictly redundant and should simply not be used), and Eq. 4/5 notation that is hard to follow without the figure.

No limitations discussion or failure-case analysis. Given that the method commits to a fixed decomposition level L and a fixed resize factor, a discussion of when frequency separation could fail (e.g., moiré energy spanning both bands) would be appropriate.

There is no clearly declared contribution type; treated as Algorithms/General, the algorithmic contribution is incremental and the strongest case for the paper rests on empirical performance, which — given the missing comparisons to P-BiC [9] and the questionable Haar baseline — is not fully established.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated: the observation that moiré textures concentrate in high-frequency bands while color distortions persist in low-frequency bands is clearly supported by the frequency-decomposition visualization (Fig. 2) and directly drives the dual-branch design.

The overall framework is coherent and practical: dilated-blur-based frequency decomposition, crop-based training for the high-frequency branch and resize-based training for the low-frequency branch, and a learnable Frequency Composition Transform (FCT) are all justified by the empirical properties of the components.

Strong empirical evidence: state-of-the-art results on FHDMi across PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS and first in SSIM/LPIPS on UHDM, all with a compact 6.065M-parameter model and low FLOPs (2.49T for 4K). Comparisons against both demoiréing specialists and recent general restoration models (AdaIR, MoCE-IR, OSEDiff) strengthen the evaluation.

Ablations are unusually thorough: the resize-vs-crop study for the low branch (Tab. 3, validated also on ESDNet-L), the learnable-vs-fixed FCT and two-stage training study (Tab. 4), per-branch comparisons at matched parameter budget (Tab. 5), component ablations (Tab. 6), and the Haar-transform comparison all support individual design choices rather than only the final system.
Efficiency is a genuine contribution for a practical task: the model is suitable for high-resolution (4K) demoiréing, which most heavier baselines handle poorly.
The paper is largely readable, with a clear pipeline description and training recipe (implementation details are specific enough to support reproducibility, and code release is promised).
weaknesses: Novelty of the frequency decomposition is limited: the transform (Eq. 1-2) is essentially a Laplacian-pyramid-style blur/high-pass split using a fixed dilated binomial kernel, explicitly adapted from prior work [37]. The contribution is more in how this decomposition is exploited for demoiréing than in the decomposition itself, which should be stated more modestly.
The claim of state-of-the-art is slightly overstated on UHDM, where Freqformer is second in PSNR (22.22 vs. 22.42 for ESDNet-L); on FHDMi the margin over ESDNet-L is real but modest (~0.4 dB).

The Haar-wavelet comparison (PSNR 13.32) is suspiciously catastrophic and reads as an unfair or under-trained baseline; a fixed-blur vs. Haar ablation controlling for all other factors would be more convincing than the reported dramatic failure.

Several claims lack clarity or rigor: Eq. 4's text says the split convolutions are 'mathematically equivalent' to concatenation yet 'doubles the number of bias parameters' (contradictory phrasing); the decomposition level L is not specified or ablated; the speed column in Tab. 6 lacks units and context; the equivalence of the two-stage training gains to design choices vs. simply more training compute is not fully disentangled.

Writing quality needs polish: informal/incorrect phrasing (e.g., 'awesome benifits', 'reals that the green channel is less effected') appears in the technical sections, and there are minor grammatical issues throughout.

The SA-CA module is an assembly of existing components (RDDB, channel attention with 1x1 + depth-wise projection, gated FFN) and its individual benefit is small (Tab. 6 shows <0.03 dB from H.F. and RDDB), so its framing as a core contribution is somewhat generous.

No limitations or failure-case discussion is provided (e.g., behavior on extreme moiré frequencies, generalization to datasets other than FHDMi/UHDM such as TIP-2018 or LCDMoiré, or sensitivity to the resize factor of the low branch).

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the method is trained and tested separately on four standard demoiréing benchmarks (TIP2018, LCDMoire, FHDMi, UHDM) and compared against both demoiréing-specific methods and general-purpose restoration models (AdaIR, MoCE-IR, OSEDiff, RRID, STD-Net, DTNet), which strengthens the state-of-the-art claim.

Strong parameter efficiency: 6.065M parameters with 2.46 TFLOPS for 4K inference, outperforming much larger methods on most benchmarks, with explicit FLOPs and inference-time reporting (including an honest admission that it is slower than ESDNet-L despite fewer FLOPs).

Thorough ablation studies covering each claimed contribution: the frequency decomposition vs. Haar DWT / Block DCT (Table 3, Fig. 7), the asymmetric crop/resize low-branch training (Table 4, including cross-verification with ESDNet-L), the learnable vs. fixed FCT (Table 5), and internal architecture choices such as hierarchical fusion, RDDB, SCP, and a DAT baseline (Table 6). This level of component-level validation is above average.

The asymmetric training scheme (crop for high-frequency, resize for low-frequency) is a sensible and well-motivated design, empirically supported by the ~29.9 vs ~23.1 dB gap in Table 4 and the supporting evidence that the low-frequency component is scale-robust (~50 dB reconstruction after resizing).
The paper is generally well organized, and the qualitative comparisons in Fig. 6 and Fig. 7 are consistent with the quantitative claims.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core frequency decomposition: it is explicitly 'inspired by Wang et al. [33]' and is essentially a fixed, dilated-convolution Gaussian blur plus subtraction, i.e., a Laplacian-pyramid-style separation. The 'learnable Frequency Composition Transform' framing oversells what is, in effect, a convolution plus a small transformer-based fusion block. The contribution is more an assembly/engineering contribution than a new algorithmic idea, which should be stated more plainly.

On the most practically relevant benchmark (UHDM, real-world 4K), Freqformer is second in PSNR to ESDNet-L (22.24 vs 22.42) and slower at inference (0.58 s vs 0.25 s/image), so the 'state-of-the-art with compact size' claim is somewhat weaker than the abstract suggests; the claimed suitability for 'edge devices' is asserted but never demonstrated (no latency/memory measurements on resource-constrained hardware).

Potential train/test inconsistency for the high-frequency branch: it is trained with random crops but tested at full resolution, and the paper does not analyze when/why this generalizes, nor discuss failure modes for very large-scale moiré patterns that the authors themselves criticize in MBCNN's restricted receptive field.

A key empirical motivation (resize of the low-frequency component preserving color information, ~50 dB) is stated with only a one-sentence summary; the experiment setup and statistics are not provided. Similarly, the decomposition level L and its sensitivity are never specified or ablated.

The paper attributes part of the low-frequency discrepancy to dataset color shifts; it is unclear how much of the low-branch gain reflects correction of a dataset artifact (lighting mismatch during capture) rather than genuine moiré color-distortion removal, raising a generalization concern to real-world deployment that is not addressed in a limitations discussion.

Ablations are performed only on FHDMi; given the different characteristics of TIP2018/LCDMoire/UHDM, at least one ablation on UHDM (the real-world 4K dataset) would substantially strengthen the evidence.

Presentation and rigor issues: informal language ('some awesome benefits are shown'), broken/incomplete abstract (code URL is cut off), minor notation inconsistencies in Eqs. 2-3, and several N/A entries in the comparison tables (e.g., ESDNet SSIM on LCDMoire) that reduce clarity about fairness of comparison protocols (whether baselines were retrained under identical settings is only partially clarified for Table 2, not Table 1).
No discussion of limitations or societal impact, and no failure-case analysis, which would be expected for the strength of claims made.

strengths: The core empirical claim is well supported: Freqformer achieves state-of-the-art or near-SOTA results across four standard demoiréing benchmarks (TIP2018, LCDMoire, FHDMi, UHDM) with a compact 6M-parameter model, and includes comparisons against both demoiréing-specific methods and general-purpose restoration models (AdaIR, MoCE-IR, OSEDiff), including retrained baselines for fairness.

The asymmetric training scheme (crop-based training for the high-frequency branch, resize-based training for the low-frequency branch) is a simple but well-motivated idea, and the ablation in Table 4 shows a surprisingly large gain (29.90 vs 23.13 dB for the low branch), also corroborated with an ESDNet-L control.

The ablation studies are thorough: they isolate the frequency decomposition choice (vs. Haar DWT and Block DCT, Table 3), the learnable FCT (Table 5), and architectural components including SA-CA, hierarchical fusion, SCP, and a DAT baseline (Table 6), each with parameter/speed accounting.

The paper is generally well organized, the motivation that moiré artifacts concentrate in high frequencies while color distortion resides in low frequencies is supported by visualization (Fig. 2), and the complexity analysis (FLOPS and inference time on 4K) is candidly reported, including admitting that Freqformer is slower than ESDNet-L despite fewer FLOPs.
weaknesses: The claimed novelty of the 'novel frequency decomposition' is overstated. The proposed transform (Eqs. 1-3) is a Laplacian-pyramid-style decomposition using a fixed Gaussian-like kernel with dilation — a very standard construction (the paper itself says it is 'inspired by Wang et al. [33]'). The learnable FCT is likewise a fairly simple concatenate-and-convolve feature fusion with a small transformer block. The individual components offer limited conceptual novelty; the contribution is more an effective engineering combination than a new method.

The motivation for rejecting Haar/DCT rests on qualitative arguments (spatial discontinuity, shift variance, block artifacts) that are asserted rather than rigorously demonstrated; the supporting evidence is mainly the final performance gap in Table 3, which confounds decomposition choice with the accompanying band-specific modules.

Some technical descriptions are imprecise or incomplete: Eq. (2) is referenced but never displayed; the notation in Eqs. 8-10 is garbled in places; the abstract ends with an incomplete sentence ('The code will be made publicly available at'); and informal phrasing such as 'some awesome benefits are shown' undermines rigor. Key hyperparameters (L, number of levels; downsampling factor 0.1x for the low branch) are not clearly stated.

The gap to the strongest competitor (ESDNet-L) is modest on UHDM (second in PSNR) and the method is slower at 4K inference (0.58 s vs 0.25 s), which weakens the efficiency claim; the paper acknowledges but does not resolve this.

Evaluation is confined to synthetic/screen-recaptured benchmark datasets; there is no evidence of generalization to in-the-wild moiré images or a user study for perceptual quality, and there is no explicit limitations discussion (e.g., sensitivity of the fixed kernel to different capture geometries).

Contribution type is Algorithms/General; judged under that framing the empirical evidence is adequate, but the conceptual advancement is incremental relative to existing frequency-aware dual-branch demoiréing networks (WDNet, MBWDN, FHDe2Net), making the paper's significance dependent on the strength of the benchmark gains.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated, practically relevant problem (image demoiréing) with a coherent design: the frequency decomposition cleanly separates moiré texture (high-frequency) from color distortion (low-frequency), and this separation directly motivates the dual-branch architecture and the asymmetric crop/resize training scheme. The design rationale is well supported by the visualization analysis in Fig. 2.

The asymmetric training strategy is well justified empirically: the ∼25 dB vs. ∼50 dB reconstruction experiment (Sec. 3.2) and the low-branch ablation (Table 4) convincingly show that resize-based training of the low-frequency branch is far superior to crop/tile alternatives, and the finding generalizes to ESDNet-L, strengthening its credibility.

Experimental evidence is broad and thorough: four standard benchmarks (TIP2018, LCDMoire, FHDMi, UHDM), comparisons against both demoiréing-specific and general-purpose restoration models (including recent 2024–2025 methods such as RRID, STD-Net, DTNet, AdaIR, MoCE-IR), and a multi-part ablation (Tables 3–6) covering the decomposition choice, FCT, hierarchical fusion, and block design. Ablations also include retraining competitor architectures under the same frequency-decomposition setting (e.g., ESDNet + FCT), which is a good practice.

The efficiency claim is credible and honest: Freqformer attains SOTA or near-SOTA results with only 6.065M parameters and 2.46 TFLOPS for 4K inference. The authors transparently report that inference is slower than ESDNet-L despite lower FLOPs and attribute it to attention operator optimization, rather than hiding this limitation.

The ablation against Haar DWT and Block DCT (Table 3, Fig. 7) directly substantiates the core claim that the proposed decomposition is better suited to demoiréing than conventional discrete transforms.
weaknesses: Novelty of the frequency decomposition is overstated. The proposed transform is essentially a dilated-convolution Gaussian-blur pyramid (Eq. 1–3), explicitly inspired by Wang et al. [33] (Real-ESRGAN-style blur-and-subtract). The paper markets this as a 'novel frequency decomposition' without adequately acknowledging how close it is to prior blur-decomposition schemes; a deeper analysis of why this specific kernel suits moiré separation (beyond visual inspection of Fig. 2) is missing.

Most ablations (Tables 3–6) are conducted only on FHDMi. Given that the paper's strongest motivation is ultra-high-resolution demoiréing, key ablations—especially the frequency decomposition comparison and the FCT design—should also be validated on UHDM, where the method is actually second in PSNR to ESDNet-L.

The learnable FCT module, while useful (+0.13–0.38 dB over fixed composition in Table 5), is architecturally modest (two convolutions plus a 2-layer transformer block), and its contribution is relatively small compared to the decomposition itself. The improvement margin of Freqformer over ESDNet-L is also small on UHDM, so claims of 'significant' superiority should be tempered.

Some method details are under-specified: the level L of the decomposition is never stated, the choice of the fixed kernel k is not justified analytically (e.g., against other blur kernels or learnable ones), and Eq. 2 uses a convolution with 'dilation rate 2^i' whose interaction with the fixed 3×3 kernel deserves more analysis (e.g., whether anti-aliasing claims hold at larger dilations).

Presentation issues: informal wording ('awesome benefits', Sec. 3.2), broken equations in the source (Eq. 8 missing from the loss definitions, malformed Eq. 3/5–7), a placeholder code URL ('will be made publicly available at'), and minor typos. These do not undermine the science but reduce polish.

External validity of the low-frequency resize strategy at inference deserves more scrutiny: the claim that Il is scale-robust is supported by a synthetic PSNR test on clean images, but behavior under extreme real-world scale variation or non-uniform moiré coverage is not analyzed. Also, the comparison to OSEDiff is arguably unfair in the opposite direction (a ~1B-parameter generative model beats Freqformer on LPIPS), which the paper handles reasonably but could discuss more.
